778.title: Jerome's Bible
778.hook: a grumpy genius in a Bethlehem cave translates the Bible into Latin
778.carry: ignorance of scripture is ignorance of christ
778.howItsDone: Christians honor Jerome as a saint and a doctor of the church, and some remember him as a patron of translators; the Vulgate remains an official Latin text of the Catholic Church, while Christians today read the Bible in many modern translations.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ambrose, and your line was no one is above it. Did an apology get said, or heard? Day seven hundred seventy-eight.

Gourd, or ivy? A letter carries that question from North Africa to Bethlehem. Augustine is writing to Jerome. A bishop in a town called Oea has had the book of Jonah read aloud in Jerome's new translation. At the moment where God makes a plant grow up to shade the sulking prophet, the congregation hears a different plant. They know it as a gourd. Jerome's version says ivy. There's an uproar in the church, Augustine says, and the bishop nearly loses his people over one word. Today's word is the Bible that word came from.

Jerome was a scholar with a sharp pen and a short temper, and his letters show both. Tradition places him in Bethlehem, working near the cave where Christians remember Jesus being born. Latin-speaking Christians already had Latin Bibles, translated from the Greek by different hands, and the copies didn't agree. Jerome set out to revise them, and then he did something bolder. For the Old Testament, he went back past the Greek to the Hebrew. In his prefaces he calls it the Hebrew truth, and he describes the hard labor of learning the language. That's how the gourd became ivy. The Hebrew word for Jonah's plant is rare, and Jerome made a choice. When Augustine wrote, worried, Jerome wrote back, not gently, and defended it. The King James translators, also working from the Hebrew, went with gourd: "And the LORD God prepared a gourd, and made it to come up over Jonah, that it might be a shadow over his head." Readers still differ on what plant it was. Here's the larger thing. Jerome's Latin went on being read and copied in the Western church long after him, and it came to be called the Vulgate. And he gave a reason for all that labor. In his commentary on Isaiah he writes that not to know the scriptures is not to know Christ. He was echoing Jesus in John's Gospel: "Search the scriptures; for in them ye think ye have eternal life: and they are they which testify of me." A Bible in anyone's own language comes through someone like Jerome, bent over a hard word, choosing gourd or ivy, and getting letters about it.

Here's the practice: thank a translator. Settle, and breathe. Who has carried words across for you? It might be a translator in the plain sense: whoever put the Bible, or any book you love, into your language, or a parent who interpreted for you at the doctor. Or someone who put a hard thing into words you could understand: a teacher, a nurse, a friend. Picture them if you can. Let a simple thanks rise. If you pray, you can thank God for them by name. If you don't, just hold the gratitude for this minute. The bell holds the time.
Vulgate. The Latin Bible tied to Jerome's work, made so people could hear scripture in the language of their own churches.

Your line: ignorance of scripture is ignorance of christ. Today, read one short passage slowly, in whatever translation you have, and find one word a translator had to choose. Day seven hundred seventy-eight.

779.title: The stolen pears (Confessions 2)
779.hook: Augustine remembers stealing pears as a boy, not from hunger, just to do wrong
779.howItsDone: Augustine's Confessions is read by Christians of different churches as a model of honest self-examination; some use the practice of examining the day, or the examination of conscience before confession, in the same spirit.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jerome's Bible, the Vulgate, and your line was ignorance of scripture is ignorance of christ. Which word did you catch a translator choosing? Day seven hundred seventy-nine.
screen: `IGNORANCE OF SCRIPTURE IS IGNORANCE OF CHRIST.`

segments.voice: It's late at night, and a gang of boys has stayed out in the streets longer than they should. Near a vineyard stands a pear tree, loaded with fruit. The pears aren't much to look at, and not much to taste. The boys shake the tree anyway and carry off armfuls. They eat a few. The rest they throw to the pigs. One of those boys grew up to be Augustine, and years later, writing his Confessions, he could not let that night go. He kept asking one question about it. Today: the stolen pears.

The Confessions is a long prayer. Augustine tells his life to God, out loud, on the page. And of everything he could linger on, he stops at a pear tree. Why? Because, he says, he wasn't hungry. He had better pears at home. He didn't want the fruit. He wanted the stealing. He loved, he says, the wrong itself. That honesty is the strange gift of this chapter. It's easy to explain small wrongs away: I was tired, I was provoked, everybody does it. Augustine refuses the excuse. He looks for the reason, and keeps looking, and the first answer he finds is ugly: he did it because it wasn't allowed. Then he finds a second. He would not, he says, have done it alone. It was the company: the laughing, the daring, the not wanting to be the one who held back. He calls it a friendship that was no friend at all. That's the turn. The theft wasn't only about pears. It was about belonging. Paul had put words to this tangle in his letter to the Romans: "for what I would, that do I not; but what I hate, that do I." Augustine gives a boyhood prank his full attention because he's digging for the root. Readers take the chapter in more than one way. Some connect it with Augustine's later teaching on the bent of the human will and on original sin. Others read it more simply, as a man telling the truth about a night he'd rather forget. Either way, he doesn't stop at the guilt. The whole book is spoken to the God he believes forgave him. Naming the wrong is the first step. Finding the reason is the second.

Here's the practice: remember a small wrong, honestly. Settle, and breathe. Let one small wrong from long ago come to mind, nothing heavy: something taken, a lie told, a cruelty you joined in. Don't defend it, and don't punish yourself with it. Just ask Augustine's question. Why did I do it? Was it the thing itself, or the doing, or the people watching? Let the real answer come up slowly. If you pray, you can tell God the reason you find. If you don't, simply let yourself know it, for this minute. The bell holds the time.
Augustine. His boyhood theft of pears, done not from hunger, but for the wrong itself, and for the company.
Your line: know why you do it. Today, before one small choice, a purchase, a reply, a joke at someone's expense, pause and ask the reason underneath. Day seven hundred seventy-nine.

780.title: Ostia (Confessions 9)
780.hook: Augustine and Monica, at a window, talk of heaven; days later she dies
780.howItsDone: Catholic, Orthodox and Anglican Christians remember Monica as a saint, often as a patron of mothers who pray for their children; the scene at Ostia is read as part of Augustine's Confessions.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Augustine, and your line was know why you do it. What reason did you find underneath a choice? Day seven hundred eighty.

Two people are leaning at a window that looks out on a garden. The house is in Ostia, the port of Rome. They're resting after a long journey overland, waiting for a ship to carry them home to Africa. One is Augustine, newly baptized. The other is his mother, Monica, who wept and prayed over him through all his wandering. Nobody else is in the room. And they begin to talk, quietly, about what the life of the saints with God might be like. Today: Ostia.

Augustine tells it in the ninth book of his Confessions. Their talk climbs, step by step. They leave behind every pleasure of the body. Then the beauty of earth and sky, sun and moon and stars. Then even their own minds, reaching toward the Wisdom by which all things are made. And for a moment, he writes, they touched it, just barely, with the whole force of the heart. Then they sighed, and came back down to the sound of their own voices, to words that have a beginning and an end. He wonders what it would be like if that moment simply went on, and he reaches for Jesus's words in Matthew's Gospel, in the King James: "enter thou into the joy of thy lord." Then Monica speaks. Son, she says, for my part nothing in this life delights me anymore. What am I still doing here? There was one thing I wanted to stay for: to see you a Christian before I died. God has given me that, and more. Days later, she falls ill with a fever. Near the end, one of her sons says he wishes she could die in her own country, not in a strange place. She waves it away. Lay this body anywhere, she says. Only remember me at the altar of the Lord, wherever you are. Augustine holds back his tears at her burial, and then, later, alone, he lets them come. Notice where this moment of reaching for God takes place. Not in a desert, not in a church. At a window, on a trip, in a borrowed house, between a mother and a son who had been far apart and found their way back. They didn't plan it. They were just talking about what mattered.

Here's the practice: get ready to talk with someone you love about what matters. Settle, and breathe. Bring that person to mind: a parent, a child, a friend, a partner. Picture the two of you at a window, with nowhere to be. What would you want to ask them? What they hope for. What they're grateful for. What they think happens at the end. Find one question. Then hear yourself asking it, gently. If you pray, you can hold that person before God. If you don't, hold them in your attention for this minute. The bell holds the time.
Ostia. The port where Augustine and Monica, at a window, reached for God together, days before she died.
Your line: at the window. Today, find a few unhurried minutes with someone you love, and ask them the question you found. Day seven hundred eighty.

781.title: Rome falls (410)
781.hook: the city is sacked, and Augustine writes City of God: two cities, two loves
781.howItsDone: Augustine's City of God is read and taught by Christians of different churches, especially when they think about faith and public life; his image of two cities and two loves is often cited in that conversation.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ostia, and your line was at the window. Who did you sit with, and what did you ask them? Day seven hundred eighty-one.

The news crosses the sea, and it's hard to believe. Rome has been sacked. An army of Goths has broken into the city and plundered it. People who fled are arriving. And some are saying out loud what they're thinking: this happened because Rome turned from its old gods to the Christian one. Across the water in Africa, Augustine is now a bishop. He hears the charge. He picks up his pen to answer it, and the answer grows into a very long book. Today: Rome falls.
screen: `THE OLD GODS, OR THE NEW ONE?`

segments.voice: The book is The City of God. Augustine starts with the charge itself. During the sack, he points out, the invaders spared people who fled into the churches of the apostles, and some of those spared are now the ones blaming Christ. Then he goes much further than a reply. There are, he says, two cities mixed together in this world. Not two places. Two loves. The Psalms sing of one of them, in the King James words: "Glorious things are spoken of thee, O city of God." Beside it Augustine sets the earthly city. And then comes the line that holds the whole book together. Two loves, he writes, have made two cities. Love of self, reaching even to contempt of God, made the earthly city. Love of God, reaching even to contempt of self, made the heavenly one. That changes the question. For Augustine, Rome was never the city of God, not even a Christian Rome. No empire is. The two cities run through every street and every church, tangled together until the end. So when Rome falls, he tells his readers, they may grieve, but their hope was not built on its walls. The letter to the Hebrews had already said it: "For here have we no continuing city, but we seek one to come." That's no excuse to stop caring about the earthly city. Augustine says the heavenly city, while it's on pilgrimage here, makes use of the earthly city's peace and seeks it, since its people share that life too. But it puts every city, every party, every institution under the same question: what does it love? And the question doesn't stop at the city limits. It runs through each person, too.
screen: `NO EMPIRE IS THE CITY OF GOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: ask which city you're building. Settle, and breathe. Think of the places your days go into: your work, your home, a group you belong to, the screen in your pocket. Pick one. Then ask Augustine's question of it, quietly. What is it built on? What does it love? And what am I adding to it: love that curls inward, or love that turns outward? Don't grade yourself. Just look. If you pray, you can offer that place to God. If you don't, simply see it clearly for this minute. The bell holds the time.
Rome falls. The sack of the city that set Augustine writing The City of God: two cities, made by two loves, mixed until the end.
Your line: two cities, two loves. Today, before you give an hour to something, ask which city it builds. Day seven hundred eighty-one.

782.title: The golden mouth
782.hook: John Chrysostom: if you can't find Christ in the beggar at the door, you won't find him in the chalice
782.howItsDone: Orthodox and Eastern Catholic churches celebrate the Divine Liturgy that bears John Chrysostom's name, and Christians of different churches honor him as a saint and read his sermons, especially on care for the poor.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rome falls, and your line was two cities, two loves. Which city did your hours build? Day seven hundred eighty-two.

Silk in the church. Gold cups for the wine. A preacher stands in a church full of beautiful things, and he points past all of it, to the door, and to the man sitting outside it, asking for bread. The preacher is John, a priest of Antioch who later became bishop of Constantinople. People came to call him Chrysostom, which means golden mouth. Today: what the golden mouth said about that door.

The sermon is one of his homilies on Matthew's Gospel. He's speaking about the bread and the cup, the body of Christ at the altar, and he speaks of it with deep reverence. Then he turns. Do you want to honor Christ's body? he asks. Then don't ignore him when he's naked. Don't honor him in here with silk, while outside you pass him by, cold and without clothes. What good is it, he says, if his table is loaded with gold cups, while he himself is dying of hunger? Feed him first when he's hungry. Then adorn his table too. He isn't against beautiful churches. He's against the order being backwards. Where does he get this? From Jesus, in Matthew. At the end of a story about the last judgment, the King says, in the King James words: "Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me." Chrysostom takes that at its word. The person at the door isn't only a reminder of Christ. By the words of that Gospel, what's done to him is done to Christ. The same Christ the congregation is about to receive at the altar is sitting outside, asking. Churches understand the altar differently. Orthodox and Catholic Christians speak of Christ truly present in the bread and wine; Protestant churches understand communion in a range of ways. All of them can hear Chrysostom's question about the door. The golden mouth didn't keep him safe. His preaching against luxury, the luxury of the powerful included, made him enemies, and he died in exile. His sermons are still read, and that question is still in them: did you see him at the door?

Here's the practice: get ready to see Christ at the door. Settle, and breathe. Recall someone you've passed who was asking: on a corner, at a station, outside a shop. Maybe you gave, maybe you looked away. No verdict either way. Just see their face again, as a face. Then decide one concrete thing for the next time: a coin, a sandwich, a question about their name. If you pray, you can pray for that person, even without a name. If you don't, keep their face in mind for this minute. The bell holds the time.
Chrysostom, the golden mouth. John, the preacher who said the Christ honored at the altar is also asking at the door.
Your line: christ at the door. Today, if someone asks you for help, give something, and look them in the eye when you do. Day seven hundred eighty-two.

783.title: Chalcedon (451)
783.hook: one person, two natures; some ancient churches did not accept the wording, and dialogue continues today
783.howItsDone: Churches that accept Chalcedon teach Christ as one person in two natures; Oriental Orthodox churches (Coptic, Armenian, Ethiopian, Eritrean, Syriac and Malankara) confess one united nature of the incarnate Word, and the two families of churches continue in dialogue.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Chrysostom, and your line was christ at the door. Who was at your door, and what did you give? Day seven hundred eighty-three.

How do you say, in one sentence, who Jesus is? Bishops have been arguing over it for a long time, and now they're gathered at Chalcedon, a city just across the water from Constantinople, to try again. The question is sharp. If Jesus is truly God, is he really human, with a human mind and a human tiredness? If he's truly human, how is he God? One side fears a Christ split in two. The other fears a Christ blended into something neither. Whole churches are listening. Today: Chalcedon.

The council's answer is short to say and hard to live inside. One and the same Christ, its definition says, truly God and truly human. Known in two natures, without confusion, without change, without division, without separation. Two natures, one person. These words work like fences around a mystery. They don't explain how. They mark where not to go. Don't blend the two into a mixture. Don't split him into two people sharing a body. Behind it all stands a line from John's Gospel, in the King James: "And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us." Catholic and Eastern Orthodox churches, and the Protestant churches that hold the early creeds, accept the Chalcedonian definition. But not everyone did. Some ancient churches, the Coptic, the Armenian, the Ethiopian and the Syriac Orthodox among them, did not accept the wording. They were not denying that Christ is fully God and fully human. They preferred to speak of one united nature of God the Word made flesh, from two, and to them two natures sounded like splitting him. Today these churches are often called the Oriental Orthodox. The parting was real, and it hurt, and it lasted. And the talking never fully stopped. In recent times, leaders and theologians from both sides have met, and some have said they confess the same Christ in different words. Full communion hasn't been restored. The conversation continues. So Chalcedon is two things at once: a definition the churches that accept it hold dear, and a parting that people on both sides are still tending. And both sides still confess the same short line: truly God, truly human.

Here's the practice: hold the churches that parted. Settle, and breathe. If you pray, you can pray for the churches that parted after Chalcedon and for the people still talking, by name if you like: Coptic, Armenian, Ethiopian, Syriac, and the churches on the other side of the table. If you don't pray, bring to mind a split you know: in a family, a friendship, a group that used to be one. Notice that each side may have been guarding something true. Hold both sides in quiet goodwill for this minute. The bell holds the time.
Chalcedon. The council that said Christ is one person in two natures, and the parting of churches that followed.
Your line: truly god, truly human. Today, when you disagree with someone, say their view back in words they'd accept, before you say yours. Day seven hundred eighty-three.

784.title: Patrick
784.hook: a British boy kidnapped to Ireland escapes, then goes back to the people who enslaved him
784.howItsDone: Catholic, Anglican, Orthodox and other Christians honor Patrick as a saint and the apostle of Ireland; his Confession is read as his own account of his captivity, escape and return.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Chalcedon, and your line was truly god, truly human. Whose view did you say back to them before your own? Day seven hundred eighty-four.

Raiders come to a family's land in Britain and carry off a boy, along with many others, across the sea to Ireland. He's put to work watching animals on the hills, alone, through rain and frost and snow. His father was a deacon, his grandfather a priest, and the boy, by his own account, had paid none of it much attention. Now, out on the hillside, he starts to pray. Years later he'll write the story himself, in rough Latin he apologizes for. Today: Patrick.

Patrick's Confession doesn't read like a legend. It reads like a man explaining his life to people who doubted him. On that hillside, he says, the love of God grew in him. He prayed through the day and into the night, in snow and frost and rain, and felt no harm. Then one night, in his sleep, he heard a voice: your ship is ready. He ran, a long way, he says, to a coast he didn't know, talked his way onto a ship, and after hard days, and some years, was home with his family again. His family begged him never to leave them again. Then came another dream. A man named Victoricus seemed to come from Ireland, carrying letters, more than could be counted. He handed one over, and at the top it said: The Voice of the Irish. As Patrick read, he heard the people from beside the western sea calling to him, as if with one voice: holy boy, we beg you, come and walk among us again. And he went back. To the land where he'd been a slave. To the people who had taken him. As a bishop he baptized and ordained, and he refused gifts, even handing back what was left on the altar, so no one could say he'd come for profit. It wasn't safe. He writes of being seized and put in chains. Jesus had said, in the King James: "Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you." Patrick doesn't cast himself as the hero. He calls himself a sinner, the least of the faithful, and gives the credit to God. The shamrock and the snakes come from later stories, not from his own pages. What his pages hold is stranger: a man who went back.
screen: `BACK TO THE PEOPLE WHO TOOK HIM.`
`NO SHAMROCK: A MAN WHO WENT BACK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: go back, gently, to a place of hurt, carrying something good. Settle, and breathe. Let a place or a person tied to an old hurt come to mind. Not the deepest one; something you can hold today. And stay safe: going back in your heart never means walking back into harm. Ask one small question. Is there a good thing I could bring there now? A kind word. A visit. Simply wishing them well, from a distance. If you pray, you can bring that place to God. If you don't, hold it in steady goodwill for this minute. The bell holds the time.
Patrick. The captive who escaped, then heard the voice of the Irish and went back. That ends a week of Jerome, the pears, Ostia, Rome, the golden mouth, Chalcedon and Patrick.
Your line: the voice of the irish. Today, think of someone you'd rather not go back to, and, if it's safe, do one small good thing in their direction. Day seven hundred eighty-four.

fork.setup: you've escaped slavery and you're home. your family begs you never to leave. then you dream that the people who held you are calling you back. what do you do?
options: stay home: you've suffered enough.
go back, to the people who enslaved you.
send someone else in your place.
fork.reveal: Patrick went back to Ireland as a bishop, to the people who had taken him, and he wasn't always safe there.

original.note: Latin, from Patrick's own Confession: the voice of the Irish, the words at the top of the letter in his dream.

trapdoor: what you thought: a saint with a shamrock and a parade.
what it means: a British captive escaped Ireland, then went back as a bishop to the people who had enslaved him.
what a scholar hears: the source is his own Confession, in rough Latin he apologizes for; the shamrock and the snakes come from later stories.
